title: Founding the Las Vegas Jazz Society in 1975
summary: Unable to do it alone, he called about 30 people to his house, set dues at $15 and $25, and grew to about 500 members.

story.theme_name: Late-career reflections: awards, legacy and life lessons
story.community_name: What's next: upcoming tours, records and plans

blocks.x: Now, I'm out there, I knew I had to fight the system. And I'm going on and I made some attempts. I tried another thing and it almost worked, at a downtown hotel where I didn't want to go at all, because what I was trying to get involved with belonged on the Strip. And I kept getting defeated there.
Anyhow, I came to the thing and I knew that one person ...I could not make a dent in anything alone. And I knew I couldn't do it one...single-handedly. That's why I formed the jazz society.
...five. '75 I formed the jazz society. And at that time I didn't realize the impact of what the jazz society was going to be. I just knew I had to get...I couldn't do it single-handedly.
How many people are there now involved? I know it's grown enormously.

Yeah, it's grown enormously. We have...we use the figure of 500 as membership, and it's hard to arrive at an exact number because we have different types of membership. On, say, a family membership, you don't know how many is in a family. And it keeps you from arriving at an exact number. We have individual, family and student. But in the neighborhood of 500, so far as how much support we have, it goes way beyond that in terms
You have a pretty strong constituency in Las Vegas...

Oh sure, because we also have...We feel like the associators, that are associated with the jazz society not as membership per se, but we feel we have the press, we have the radio, television, newspapers, which cover so greatly...
An involvement which you couldn't get as an individual...

Right. You can't count that in memberships, but they'll keep you in the eye of the public, to get the support back in return. We feel like we're so strongly supported in the community that it's hard to arrive at any numbers...
The political credibility that you've gained, with things like the state-wide Jazz Month...
All those things came about in good time...
...has given you a lot of strength to use in other areas.

An aful lot. In fact, we are developing to a sort of leadership on a regional level through the efforts of the jazz society. And at early stages of the jazz society, I think the curiosity of it happening sort of attracted a lot of attention.

And the way it came about, like I say, in founding the jazz society I just got on the phone and called...I had a list of about 30 some-odd people and thinking that I knew they could appreciate some jazz action of some sort in town, and asked them to meet at my house. The turnout wasn't near as great as I hoped. They just didn't show up -- it was Sunday afternoon.

I didn't let that discourage me because I asked each one of them to call three people and we would try again the following Sunday. Because some of the people that showed up were the people that would be interested.

The next, following Sunday we had a much better turnout, so we knew what we had. And it turned out to be a little fun thing, discussing it. But it began to dawn on me now, this thing, what we were shaping. That afternoon we come up with the name, which was very simple, there wasn't no big thing about that. And we discussed it thoroughly, to the point that we had to have a board and officers and so-and-so. And I suggested that what we would do was, as many as was there that day was to join, we hadn't arrived at what the membership fee was, but we pulled it together that day. Put the membership at
$15, and $25 a family. And really, that was decided right then and there on the spot for membership. Because we said, 'Let's do something, let's move on it today, just put it in some kind of...'
